# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
## Overall assessment

This is a good follow-up. It does what the earlier documents called for:

- It uses a stricter hours measure (system logs).
- It registers the meetings test before seeing the outcomes.
- It reports the counter arm's termination openly.
- It treats the Halden survivors as an upper bound, not an estimate for organisations in general.
- Its rebuttals of the Varga & Holm comment and of the meta-analysis's duration claim are largely fair.

The arithmetic holds. The main problems are four:

1. Two control offices changed their own practices mid-trial, which contaminates the control group and may explain part of the apparent decline.
2. The mediation result is stated more strongly than seven offices per arm can support.
3. It is unclear what the log-hours measure actually captures.
4. The Summary compares figures from two different hours measures.

## Arithmetic checks (pass)

- **Per-hour gains at 24 months.** On timesheets, 0.966/0.88 gives +9.8%. On logs, 0.966/0.89 gives +8.5%.
- **Halden continuers.** Hours fell from 40.3 to 34.9, a 13.4% fall. Output per hour is 96.8/86.6, a gain of 11.8%.
- **Mediation shares.** 47% + 18% + 35% = 100%.
- **Confidence intervals.** These are symmetric on the log scale.
- **Counter arm.** The figure of "12% more staff" matches the nine-month data. Output per employee fell 11.4%, and restoring it requires 1/0.886, which is 12.9% more staff.

## Main issues

**1. The control group was contaminated, and this may account for part of the decline.**
In month 15, two of the seven control offices cut their recurring meetings. Their output per hour rose 4.1%. That improvement narrows the treated-versus-control gap from month 15 onward. Some of the fall from 12.5% to 9.8% may therefore reflect controls improving, not treated offices fading.

The report treats this episode only as evidence that reorganisation without shorter hours might work. It should also re-estimate the 24-month effect with those two offices excluded, or with a term for the audit. Spillover is also worth asking about: did the control offices get the idea from watching the treated ones?

**2. The size of the decline is overstated in places.**
- **The Summary mixes measures.** It reports a fall "from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months", but those figures come from timesheets and system logs respectively. The like-for-like comparison, given correctly in Section 3, is 12.5% to 9.8% on timesheets. That is a fall of about a fifth, not the "about a quarter" claimed in Section 5, and not the roughly one-third implied by the Summary.
- **The decline was not tested.** The 9-month and 24-month intervals overlap almost entirely (6.9–18.4 against 4.6–15.2). "Consistent with some fading" is fair. But Section 5 states the decline as a finding, and the data are equally consistent with little or no decline.
- **A cleaner comparison is probably available.** If the case-management system kept logs throughout, a 9-month log-based estimate could be computed retrospectively. That would give a like-for-like decay comparison on the stricter measure.

**3. "Confirms" is too strong for the mediation result.**
- **Effective sample size.** It is 14 offices, not the "larger sample of office-months". Months within the same office are not independent. With 7 offices per arm, an interval of 28–66% for the meetings share looks too narrow. The report should state how clustering was handled. With this few clusters, wild bootstrap or randomisation inference is again appropriate.
- **The test was not independent of the original finding.** The hypothesis came from the same seven treated offices, and the registered test was filed after the nine-month result. Registration rules out choosing the analysis after seeing the outcome. It does not make this an independent replication.
- **Mediation needs strong assumptions.** It requires no unmeasured mediator–outcome confounding, which the Limitations section concedes. The two mediators also plausibly affect each other: fewer meetings likely means less fatigue. The order in which they enter the model affects how the shares are split, and the shares are additive only if the two do not interact.

"Supports" would be accurate. "Confirms" is not, and the Summary uses it.

**4. A simple accounting check conflicts with the mediation shares.**
Using the paper's own figures:

| | Baseline | Month 24 |
|---|---|---|
| Treated hours (timesheets) | 37.9 | ≈33.4 (−12%) |
| Treated meeting hours | 7.4 | 3.9 |
| Non-meeting hours | 30.5 | ≈29.5 (−3.3%) |

Control offices changed little: their meeting time fell 0.2 hours. Output per FTE fell 3.4% relative to control. So **output per non-meeting hour is essentially unchanged.** Almost the entire per-hour gain corresponds to meeting time removed.

This is a descriptive calculation, not a causal estimate. Meetings may have had some value, and timesheet and log hours differ. Still, it suggests the meetings share could be well above 47%, leaving little room for fatigue or other pathways. The authors should reconcile the two.

**5. It is unclear what the log measure counts.**
"Active log-in time on the case-management system" counts time spent on cases. It presumably excludes meetings, email and other off-system work. That raises three problems:
- **Two different denominators.** If logs count only case work, then "actual hours, system logs −11%" measures something different from total hours worked. It is therefore not a stricter version of the timesheet measure.
- **A contradiction.** The report says logs show *more* work than timesheets. That is hard to square with logs excluding meetings, unless they capture substantial unclaimed case work.
- **A circular mediation outcome.** The mediation outcome is output per log-measured hour. If logs exclude meetings, cutting meetings would not mechanically raise that ratio. The meetings pathway would then have to work by reducing interruptions or fragmentation.

The authors should define the measure, say whether meeting time is added to it, and say whether pre-period logs exist for the difference-in-differences.

**6. The Halden subset reclassifies a case after the fact.**
The Summary says all three reverting organisations had "client-facing or coverage obligations". One was a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Under the coverage-bound versus discretionary typology used by Varden and the meta-analysis, marketing counts as discretionary. Folding it into "coverage obligations" stretches the category to fit the result. It is better reported as a discretionary organisation that reverted.

There is also response selection to note. Only 14 of the 23 organisations agreed to provide data, so on top of being "survivors twice over", the subset is selected a third time.

## Smaller points

- **Mismatched sick-day comparison.** In Table 1, the nine-month −29% was pooled across both strata in the original report. Here it sits in a case-processing-only column next to a case-processing-only −27%. The two figures are not comparable.
- **No uncertainty reported for some outcomes.** Resignations and appeal overturn rates are still raw comparisons without intervals.
- **Backlogs are still missing.** The nine-month report raised whether backlogs might build past statutory deadlines. Two years of queue-length and case-age data presumably now exist and should be reported.
- **Correcting the record.** R. Okafor is a co-author here, which is a chance to correct the Halden working paper's statement that the nine withdrawals happened "during the preparation phase". Varga & Holm showed seven occurred after the schedule began. The follow-up doesn't address this. A short correction note would help.
- **The rebuttals.** They are fair, with two qualifications:
  - **Varga & Holm.** The rebuttal shows a gain remains in one public employer's discretionary work. It does not show that gains exist generally. Varga & Holm's coverage-bound conclusion is in fact supported by the counter arm's termination.
  - **Meta-analysis.** The rebuttal on duration is strong. All four long-follow-up studies being uncontrolled and using scheduled hours confirms the confounding I flagged in my review of the meta-analysis.

## Updated picture across the five documents

| Question | Current best answer | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Per-hour gain, discretionary work | ~8–10% at 24 months (Varden, logs); 12.5% at 9 months | Reasonably supported; one employer |
| Does it decay? | Possibly modestly, by about a fifth; not tested, and partly confounded by control-office meeting cuts | Open |
| Per-worker output, discretionary | About −2 to −3%, CI includes 0 | Consistent across sources |
| Coverage-bound work | Output −9 to −11%; service worsens; restoring it costs ~9% per contact | Well supported (counter arm ended) |
| Mechanism | Meeting reduction is the largest measured pathway; fatigue is smaller | Supported, not confirmed |
| Could the gain be had without cutting hours? | Untested; two uncontrolled offices suggest partly | Open: needs a "reorganise only" arm |

The most useful next study follows directly from the unplanned observation. It would be a three-arm trial: reduced hours, meeting and workflow reorganisation at unchanged hours, and control. That would test whether the hours cut produces the gain itself or mainly serves as a forcing device for reorganisation.

I can draft a reviewer report, a correction note for the Halden paper, or an outline of that three-arm design if useful.
